title: The Firebird and the Island: Petersburg, Paris, Hollywood, San Michele
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Oranienbaum: birth on the Gulf of Finland
stops.date_confidence: attested: 17 June New Style, 5 June Old Style, 1882, at the family's summer lodging in Oranienbaum. The exact house is not identified in any source reached here; the town-centre coordinate is used.
stops.campa: West of the capital, in the Baltic resort where the imperial families take their summers, a third son is born to Fyodor Stravinsky and his wife Anna. The father is a bass at the Mariinsky, a singer of Varlaam and of Mephistopheles, with some eight thousand volumes in the house. The child is carried to Saint Petersburg and baptised into the Orthodox Church at St Nicholas Cathedral, and given the name Igor Fyodorovich. The imperial calendar dates the birth to the fifth of June, the calendar the rest of Europe keeps to the seventeenth. Abroad he will keep the seventeenth.
suggested_refs: The Stravinsky family's summer lodging at Oranienbaum, now Lomonosov
St Nicholas Naval Cathedral, Saint Petersburg, where the child was baptised
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the Mariinsky: the man across the foyer
stops.date_confidence: the boyhood attendance at his father's theatre is attested in general terms across the 1880s and 1890s; the date is an ordering device with month and day defaulted to 01. The sighting of Tchaikovsky is preserved only in Stravinsky's own later recollection and has no second witness.
stops.campa: The boy is taken into his father's theatre, blue and gold, and watches the imperial repertory from the wings and from the box before any teacher has touched him. Piano lessons begin at home around his ninth year. At one performance he is shown, across the foyer, a grey-haired man he is told is Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, who dies within weeks of the sighting. The story has no second witness; it is his alone. Sixty years on he builds a whole ballet out of Tchaikovsky's piano pieces and songs.
suggested_refs: The Mariinsky Theatre repertory of the 1880s and 1890s, in which Fyodor Stravinsky sang the leading bass roles
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the Twelve Collegia: law without a diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years 1901-1905; the month of enrolment is not established in the pool and is defaulted to September. His schooling at the Second Saint Petersburg Gymnasium on Kazanskaya Street, 1892-1901, is confirmed by the gymnasium's own pupil lists.
stops.campa: He enrols in the law faculty of the imperial university, in the long red range of the Twelve Collegia on the Neva embankment, because a gentleman's son studies law. Nine indifferent years at the Second Gymnasium lie behind him, out of which came one friendship that decides everything: Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father is the most authoritative composer in Russia. He attends lectures for four years. Music takes every hour the faculty does not claim, and he never sits the final state examination.
suggested_refs: The Twelve Collegia of Saint Petersburg University, seat of the law faculty
The Second Saint Petersburg Gymnasium, Kazanskaya ulitsa 27
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Heidelberg: the manuscripts shown to Rimsky-Korsakov
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1902; the month is a reasonable placement and the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Fyodor Stravinsky is dying of cancer in Saint Petersburg. His son travels to a German university town with Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov and lays his manuscripts in front of Vladimir's father. Do not go to the Conservatory, the old man tells him, they will crush you there; come to me privately instead. The father dies that year. The private lessons begin and run until Rimsky-Korsakov's own death in June 1908, and they are the whole of Stravinsky's formal training.
suggested_refs: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov's private teaching, 1902-1908, the whole of Stravinsky's formal training
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

segments.name: The Law Abandoned, the Estate at Ustyluh

stops.name: Saint Petersburg: the closed university and the cousin
stops.date_confidence: attested: the engagement is announced in August 1905 and the marriage takes place 24 January 1906 at a church outside the capital, whose exact location is not established in the pool. The stop is dated to the engagement.
stops.campa: The year opens with troops firing on a petition outside the Winter Palace and closes with the universities shut. His faculty never properly reconvenes; he is handed a half-diploma without sitting the examination, and no legal career ever begins. In August he announces his engagement to Yekaterina Nosenko, his first cousin, known to him since childhood. Orthodox canon forbids the marriage. A dispensation is obtained and a willing priest found in a village outside the capital, and in January they marry with none of the older generation present.
suggested_refs: The clerical dispensation for a first-cousin marriage, obtained 1905-1906

stops.name: Ustyluh: the estate in Volhynia
stops.date_confidence: attested for recurring summers, roughly 1890 to 1914; the Ustyluh article confirms frequent visits across those years. The date is an ordering device, month and day chosen for the summer season.
stops.campa: On the Bug at the western edge of the empire stands the Nosenko family estate, where he has summered since boyhood and where he now builds a house of his own. Winters are for Saint Petersburg and later for Paris; the summers here are for composition. Fyodor is born in 1907 and Ludmila in 1908. The Firebird, Petrushka and the first pages of the Rite are worked out at this table. He returns every year until 1914. After the revolution the estate stands across a frontier he cannot cross, and whatever was left in the house is lost.
suggested_refs: The Stravinsky house at Ustyluh, Volyn Oblast, reconstructed and opened as a museum
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Saint Petersburg: the Court Orchestra plays him through
stops.date_confidence: attested: the hearing of 27 April 1907 by the Court Orchestra under Hugo Wahrlich was private, not public. The first public performance of the Symphony in E flat waited until 22 January 1908, under Felix Blumenfeld. The venue of the private hearing is not named in the pool; a general Saint Petersburg coordinate is used.
stops.campa: The Symphony in E flat and the song cycle The Faun and the Shepherdess are played through by the Court Orchestra under Hugo Wahrlich, in a hearing closed to the public. Rimsky-Korsakov is there, and his name stands on the symphony's dedication. What the twenty-four-year-old hears is a competent student symphony written in his teacher's manner, and he knows it. The public hears the piece nine months later, on the twenty-second of January 1908, under Felix Blumenfeld.
suggested_refs: Symphony in E flat, Op. 1, dedicated to Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov

stops.name: Saint Petersburg Conservatory: the funeral song for the teacher
stops.date_confidence: attested: premiered 17 January 1909 in the Grand Hall of the Saint Petersburg Conservatory, Sheremetev orchestra under Felix Blumenfeld. The orchestral parts were found in a Conservatory store in spring 2015 by the librarian Irina Sidorenko, identified by the musicologist Natalya Braginskaya, and played again on 2 December 2016.
stops.campa: Rimsky-Korsakov dies in June 1908 and his pupil writes a funeral song for orchestra: all the instruments of the orchestra filing past the tomb in turn, each laying down its own melody like a wreath. Blumenfeld conducts it in the Grand Hall with the Sheremetev players. Stravinsky remembers it decades later as the best thing he made before the Firebird, and believes the score burned in the revolution. The parts sit in a Conservatory cupboard for ninety-nine years. A librarian finds them in 2015 and the piece is heard again in 2016.
suggested_refs: Chant funebre, Op. 5, rediscovered 2015 at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory and re-premiered by the Mariinsky Orchestra under Valery Gergiev, 2 December 2016

stops.name: Saint Petersburg: the impresario in the hall
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1909; the day of the concert is not established in the pool and is defaulted to 01. The concert hall is not named; a general Saint Petersburg coordinate is used.
stops.campa: At a February concert the Scherzo fantastique and Feu d'artifice are played, two short brilliant orchestral pieces by a man nobody outside the city has heard of. Sergei Diaghilev is in the hall. He has a Paris season to fill and a settled habit of hiring the unknown on purpose. Within weeks Stravinsky is orchestrating two Chopin numbers for Les Sylphides, and when Liadov proves too slow with a folk-tale ballet the whole commission comes to him instead. He is twenty-six when the letter arrives.
suggested_refs: Scherzo fantastique, Op. 3, and Feu d'artifice, Op. 4, the pieces that reached Diaghilev

segments.name: Paris: Three Ballets and a Riot That Was Not One

stops.name: Palais Garnier: the Firebird
stops.date_confidence: attested: 25 June 1910 at the Palais Garnier, not the Chatelet; the whole 1910 Ballets Russes season was at the Opera.
stops.campa: The Ballets Russes opens its second Paris season with The Firebird: Fokine's choreography, Golovin's decor, Tamara Karsavina in the title role. Anna Pavlova had been offered the part and refused it, unable to find any dance inside a score whose bars would not hold still. Karsavina takes it. Paris takes Stravinsky, unknown outside Russia in June and by the end of the season the composer everybody wants. His third child, Soulima, is born at Lausanne that same year.
suggested_refs: The 1910 Ballets Russes season at the Paris Opera

stops.name: Theatre du Chatelet: Petrushka
stops.date_confidence: attested: 13 June 1911, Theatre du Chatelet. The orchestration was finished in Rome that spring while the company played the international exhibition there.
stops.campa: It begins as a concert piece for piano and orchestra, a puppet come to life and tormenting the players with arpeggios; Diaghilev hears him play it through and demands a ballet instead. He finishes the scoring in a Rome hotel room and brings it to the Chatelet. Vaslav Nijinsky goes inside the straw suit, Fokine makes the dances, Alexandre Benois builds the Shrovetide fair, Pierre Monteux conducts. Nobody calls it a scandal. Two keys sound at once through the whole of it, C major against F sharp, and that is what the puppet is made of.
suggested_refs: The Petrushka chord, C major against F sharp major, and Benois's Shrovetide fair designs
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees: the Rite of Spring
stops.date_confidence: attested: 29 May 1913. The scale of the disorder is contested. Contemporary notices do not use the word riot; scholarship traces that framing to reviews of the 1924 revival, eleven years later.
stops.campa: The house is new, the orchestra numbers ninety-nine, Monteux conducts, Vaslav Nijinsky has made the dance and Nicholas Roerich the scenario and the clothes. The noise begins in the introduction and grows through the curtain. Nijinsky stands in the wings shouting counts to dancers who cannot hear him. About forty people are put out of the theatre. The performance runs to its end without a break. Richard Taruskin has argued that what appalled the house was the earthbound stomping on the stage rather than anything in the pit.
stops.quote: a musical-choreographic work, [representing] pagan Russia ... unified by a single idea: the mystery and great surge of the creative power of Spring
stops.quote_source: Stravinsky, note to the conductor Serge Koussevitzky, February 1914, describing The Rite of Spring; the bracketed word is an editorial insertion in the source
suggested_refs: First-night notices of Le Sacre du printemps, 29 May 1913, read against the 1924 revival reviews
Millicent Hodson's reconstruction of Nijinsky's 1913 choreography, premiered by the Joffrey Ballet 30 September 1987

stops.name: Saint Petersburg: the Rite without dancers
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates the first concert performance to 18 February 1914 under Serge Koussevitzky and places it at Saint Petersburg; other accounts of the 1914 concert premieres name Moscow first, and the hall is not established. The Philharmonia Grand Hall coordinate is used as the best available estimate.
stops.campa: Eight months after the uproar the score is played with no dancers on any stage, Koussevitzky conducting, and it is a plain success. He had spent five weeks in bed with typhoid after the Paris season. Students carry the composer out of the hall on their shoulders. He takes away the lesson he will repeat for the rest of his life: the music is sufficient in itself, and the theatre was an accident of its first appearance. From this evening the Rite is a concert work.
suggested_refs: The 1914 concert premiere of Le Sacre du printemps under Serge Koussevitzky

stops.name: Kyiv: the last summer inside Russia
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1914, the final prewar visit to Ustyluh and Kyiv; the day is not established and is defaulted to 01. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, within the same month.
stops.campa: He crosses eastward in July to fetch texts for a wedding cantata sketched the previous year, to Ustyluh first and then to Kyiv, where he buys the Kireyevsky collection of Russian village songs. In May he had staged Le Rossignol at the Paris Opera, an opera begun in 1908 and abandoned when the Firebird commission arrived, its two halves five years apart in manner and not pretending otherwise. He is back in Switzerland when Austria declares war on Serbia. He does not stand on Russian ground again for forty-eight years. The Kyiv books become Les Noces, nine years later.
suggested_refs: The Kireyevsky collection of Russian village wedding songs, source of the text of Les Noces
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

segments.name: The Swiss Years: A Household of Six and No Orchestra

stops.name: Clarens: the borders close
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1914-1915 at Clarens; the month of settling is not established and is defaulted to September, after the outbreak of war. His daughter Maria Milena was born at Leysin, where Catherine was under sanatorium treatment for tuberculosis, earlier in 1914.
stops.campa: The family came to Switzerland for a wife's lungs and stays because the frontiers have shut. At Clarens on the lake, where he had drafted the Rite two winters earlier in a room he described as scarcely bigger than a cupboard, Stravinsky settles a household of six on royalties that no longer arrive from Russia. The great ballets want a hundred players and there are no hundred players to be had anywhere in Europe now. He begins writing for whatever a village hall can hold: four singers, a handful of winds, one percussionist.
suggested_refs: The room at Clarens where the Rite of Spring was drafted in the winter of 1912-1913
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Morges: the circle on the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence 1915-1920 at Morges; month and day are not established and are defaulted to 01-01. Renard was completed in 1916. The exact villa is not confirmed and a town coordinate is used.
stops.campa: On the other shore the family takes a house at Morges and stays five years. The working circle that gathers is Swiss rather than Russian: Ernest Ansermet, who conducts him; Charles Ferdinand Ramuz, who turns his Russian folk texts into French; Werner Reinhart, the Winterthur merchant, who pays. Renard is finished in 1916, a barnyard tale for four men's voices and a cimbalom. In 1917 the revolution ends the Russian rents, and no income reaches him from home again.
suggested_refs: The Ramuz and Ansermet collaborations of the Morges years, 1915-1920
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Rome: the portrait taken for a map
stops.date_confidence: the meeting with Picasso in Italy in 1917 is carried by the dossier and by the Boosey timeline; the month is not established and is defaulted. The customs anecdote is reconstruction: memoirists tell it in several incompatible versions and no primary account was reached here.
stops.campa: Travelling with Diaghilev's company he meets Pablo Picasso, who is in Rome designing Parade for the same impresario. Picasso draws him: a few lines, a face, a collar. The story told afterwards, by more than one memoirist and never twice the same way, is that customs officers at a frontier seized the drawing as a coded plan of fortifications, refusing to accept that a portrait might look like that. Three years later Picasso designs Pulcinella for him.
suggested_refs: Picasso's line portraits of Stravinsky, 1917 and after
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky
dossier, igor_stravinsky, Swiss exile section (reconstruction, unconfirmed)

stops.name: Lausanne: the soldier and the fiddle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 28 September 1918 at Lausanne; the exact theatre is not confirmed in the pool and a city coordinate is used.
stops.campa: Seven players, three actors, a dancer and a cart: a soldier sells his fiddle to the devil, in a Russian tale moved into the Vaud and built to be carried from village to village. Reinhart pays for everything, Ansermet conducts, Ramuz has written the words. It opens at Lausanne on the twenty-eighth of September. The tour it was built for dies within days: the influenza reaching Switzerland that autumn closes the halls and puts most of the company to bed. The piece never leaves the town it opened in.
suggested_refs: L'Histoire du soldat, Lausanne, 28 September 1918, funded by Werner Reinhart
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

segments.name: Pulcinella: The Discovery of the Past

stops.name: Palais Garnier: Pulcinella
stops.date_confidence: attested: 15 May 1920 at the Paris Opera, with Picasso's designs and Leonide Massine's choreography. The music, presented at the time as Pergolesi's, was later shown to be by several eighteenth-century hands.
stops.campa: Diaghilev puts a bundle of eighteenth-century Neapolitan manuscripts in front of him, all of it then given to Pergolesi and much of it by other men, and asks for an arrangement. What comes back is not an arrangement. The old bass lines stand where they stood and the harmony beneath them has been pushed a half-step out of true; a trombone and a double bass hold a duet no eighteenth century would have tolerated. Picasso designs it and Massine choreographs it. Diaghilev, who had wanted a pastiche, is reported to have been furious.
suggested_refs: The Neapolitan manuscripts Diaghilev collected in Italy, source of the Pulcinella score
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Garches: the Villa Bel Respiro
stops.date_confidence: attested: the introduction is dated to spring 1920 and the tenancy at Bel Respiro runs September 1920 to May 1921. The alleged affair is not settled: Chanel asserted it in old age to Paul Morand, Vera Stravinsky and Robert Craft denied it, and no contemporary document decides it.
stops.campa: Diaghilev brings him in the spring to Gabrielle Chanel, and by September Stravinsky, Catherine and their four children are living in her villa outside Paris at her expense, refugees from a revolution with nowhere to go and no income. Chanel has just underwritten the Ballets Russes revival of the Rite with three hundred thousand francs on condition that nobody be told who paid. Chanel says in old age that the arrangement was also an affair. His family denies it. No letter anyone has produced decides it.
suggested_refs: Villa Bel Respiro at Garches, and the anonymous funding of the 1920 revival of Le Sacre du printemps

stops.name: Biarritz: two households and a machine
stops.date_confidence: attested: the move to the Basque coast is dated May 1921 and the Pleyel contract to the same year. The studio at the Pleyel building on the Rue Rochechouart, held roughly 1921-1933, is carried as reconstruction: the pool tags it R.
stops.campa: The household moves to the Basque coast and stays there and at Anglet for three years. In the same season Vera de Bosset, married to the painter Sudeikin, becomes his mistress; Catherine is told, and the two households run in parallel for eighteen years, both women writing to him, neither of them leaving. He signs with the Pleyel firm to cut his entire output onto rolls for their mechanical piano and keeps a studio at their Paris works, where his own tempi go into the perforated paper.
stops.quote: In the spring of 1921 a Paris music hall asked me if I could let them have a few pages of incidental music for a little sketch, within the range of their audience. It amused me to try my hand at that sort of thing, and I therefore orchestrated four pieces taken from my collections of Easy Duets.
stops.quote_source: Stravinsky, Chronicle of My Life (An Autobiography), 1936, on the origin of the Suite for Small Orchestra
suggested_refs: The Pleyela piano rolls cut by Stravinsky from 1921, and the Pleyel studio on the Rue Rochechouart
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Theatre de la Gaite-Lyrique: Les Noces
stops.date_confidence: attested: 13 June 1923 at the Theatre de la Gaite, Ballets Russes, choreography by Bronislava Nijinska. The work was conceived in 1913, not 1914, and the short score was complete by October 1917; the scoring took another six years.
stops.campa: The wedding cantata begun ten years earlier is finished at last, after four abandoned orchestrations, as four pianos, percussion, four soloists and chorus. It is a Russian village wedding in which nobody's consent is asked for or given, only lament and drink and the ritual going forward on its rails. Bronislava Nijinska sets it in brown and white, the dancers massed into blocks and pillars rather than lines. Diaghilev, who waited a decade for the score, calls it among the most important things his company ever put onto a stage.
suggested_refs: Bronislava Nijinska's choreography for Les Noces, 1923

stops.name: Palais Garnier: at the piano himself
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Concerto for Piano and Wind Instruments premiered 22 May 1924 at the Palais Garnier, Stravinsky as soloist, Koussevitzky conducting. The Capriccio, sometimes attached to 1924, belongs to 6 December 1929 under Ansermet in Paris.
stops.campa: He walks onto the stage of the Opera as a soloist for the first time, at forty-one, to play the piano part of his own concerto with Koussevitzky conducting. There are no strings in the orchestra beyond the double basses, and the piano is handled as one more percussion instrument set among the winds. For five years he will let nobody else play it. He has memorised the part and loses it in the middle of the slow movement; Koussevitzky leans over and whispers the opening notes, and he goes on.
suggested_refs: Concerto for Piano and Wind Instruments, Palais Garnier, 22 May 1924
sources: Wikipedia, 'Concerto for Piano and Wind Instruments'
Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Nice: the priest and the psalms
stops.date_confidence: attested: the move to Nice is dated September 1924 and the meeting with Father Nicolas to 1926. The Symphony of Psalms premiered in December 1930; the pool leaves the city open between Brussels and Boston and that contradiction is not resolved here.
stops.campa: The family takes a flat in Nice and keeps it a decade, the longest settled address of the French years. He works at a bare table with an upright piano and a rank of coloured inks laid out in order. Catherine and the children are here, Vera is in Paris, and the tours run across Europe and America. In 1926 he meets a priest, Father Nicolas, and returns to the Orthodox Church after thirty years outside it. Four years later he sets three psalms in Latin for chorus and an orchestra with no violins and no violas.
suggested_refs: Symphony of Psalms, 1930, composed to the glory of God and dedicated to the Boston Symphony Orchestra
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Paris: Oedipus Rex in a dead language
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1927 in Paris, in concert form, on the Ballets Russes anniversary programme; the pool does not name the theatre, so the canonical Paris pin is used rather than a guessed venue.
stops.campa: Jean Cocteau writes the libretto in French and Stravinsky has it turned into Latin, a language nobody in the house will follow word by word, so that the singers stand as monuments instead of behaving as characters. It is given in concert between two ballets, the soloists motionless. The audience is baffled and the evening is judged a failure. Stravinsky puts it among his best work and never changes his mind. Diaghilev, who had wanted a spectacle for his anniversary, calls it in private a very macabre gift.
suggested_refs: The Latin text of Oedipus Rex, translated from Cocteau's French by Jean Danielou
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt: Apollon musagete
stops.date_confidence: attested: the world premiere was 27 April 1928 at the Library of Congress, Washington, with choreography by Adolph Bolm; the Balanchine version for the Ballets Russes came 12 June 1928 at the Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt. This stop is the Paris evening, which is the one Stravinsky attended.
stops.campa: A string orchestra, three muses, one god, white tunics and nothing else on the stage. Washington saw it first in April, under Adolph Bolm; this is the version that lasts, made by the twenty-four-year-old George Balanchine. Stravinsky finds in him a dancer's mind that reads a score the way he writes one, by counting. Diaghilev watches the last rehearsal and backs a language that is not his own taste. Orpheus and Agon are thirty years ahead; the two men work together until Stravinsky's death.
suggested_refs: Apollon musagete, Library of Congress, 27 April 1928, and the Balanchine version of 12 June 1928

stops.name: Paris: Le Baiser de la fee and the end of the patron
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1928 in Paris, commissioned by Ida Rubinstein; the pool gives the month but not the day, which is defaulted to 01, and does not name the theatre.
stops.campa: Ida Rubinstein commissions a ballet for her own company and he answers with Tchaikovsky: piano pieces and songs by the man he saw once across the Mariinsky foyer as a child, taken apart and rebuilt into an Andersen story of a fairy who kisses a child and comes back for him grown. The reception is poor. Diaghilev, who does not share his composers, is reported furious that the commission was accepted at all. Nine months later the impresario dies of diabetes in Venice, aged fifty-seven.
suggested_refs: Le Baiser de la fee, on themes of Tchaikovsky, commissioned by Ida Rubinstein

stops.name: Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore: a French passport
stops.date_confidence: attested: naturalisation as a French citizen in June 1934; the day is not established and is defaulted to 01. The Faubourg Saint-Honore apartment is dated 1933-1934 by the Boosey timeline. Chroniques de ma vie appeared in two volumes in 1935 and 1936, not in 1934.
stops.campa: He takes a Paris apartment on the Faubourg Saint-Honore and in June becomes a French citizen, twenty years after a war shut him out of Russia and seventeen after a revolution took the estate. He stands for a seat at the Institut the same year and is not elected. The autobiography is in preparation, drafted with Walter Nouvel holding the pen, and comes out in two volumes in 1935 and 1936. One sentence in it will be quoted back at him for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: Music is, by its very nature, essentially powerless to express anything at all.
stops.quote_source: Stravinsky, An Autobiography (English translation of Chroniques de ma vie), 1936, pp. 53-54
suggested_refs: Chroniques de ma vie, two volumes, 1935 and 1936, drafted with Walter Nouvel
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

segments.name: Buenos Aires, and the Year Everything Goes

stops.name: Beccar, Villa Ocampo: rehearsing above the river
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ocampo was introduced to Stravinsky in Paris in 1932 by Ernest Ansermet and hosted him and his son Soulima at Villa Ocampo before the Colon premiere. The exact days of the stay are not established; the month is dated to the rehearsal period before 17 May.
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo, introduced to him in Paris four years earlier by Ernest Ansermet, brings the composer and his pianist son Soulima to her house on the bluff at Beccar, above the brown river. They rehearse in the drawing room. Persephone wants a woman who can speak French verse in strict rhythm across an orchestra, and Ocampo, forbidden the stage by her father since girlhood, has the voice and the nerve for it. She learns the part in her own house. The manuscript he later gives her carries a dedication dated the seventeenth of May.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, Elortondo 1811, Beccar, where Persephone was rehearsed
Stravinsky's manuscript of Persephone, dedicated to Victoria Ocampo, 17 May 1936

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Teatro Colon: Persephone spoken
stops.date_confidence: attested: 17 May 1936 at the Teatro Colon, with Ocampo speaking the title role.
stops.campa: He gives Persephone at the Colon with Victoria Ocampo speaking the title role, the single night of her life on which the vocation her father had threatened to shoot himself over is publicly permitted her. The text is Andre Gide's, and Gide and Stravinsky have already quarrelled over it: the poet wanted his syllables respected, the composer set them as he pleased. Buenos Aires hears the piece a year after Paris and likes it no better. Ocampo calls the evening, decades afterwards, the most painfully happy memory of her life.
stops.quote: Perséfone es el recuerdo más dolorosamente feliz de mi vida.
stops.quote_source: Victoria Ocampo, late-life reminiscence, quoted in Radio Perfil, '7 de abril de 1890 nació Victoria Ocampo'
suggested_refs: The Teatro Colon premiere of Persephone, 17 May 1936

stops.name: France: three graves in seven months
stops.date_confidence: attested that his daughter Ludmila, his wife Catherine and his mother Anna all died in 1939 or the months immediately before, all of tuberculosis in the first two cases, and that he sailed for the United States in September. The pool gives only France as the place and no burial site; the canonical Paris pin is used rather than a guessed sanatorium.
stops.campa: Tuberculosis takes his eldest daughter Ludmila, and then Catherine, his wife of thirty-three years and his cousin since childhood. His mother Anna dies in the same stretch of months. He has the disease himself and spends five months in a sanatorium. He is fifty-seven, and the household in France is finished. In September Germany invades Poland and he sails for New York with a Harvard lectureship, a case of scores, and no one left to bring. Vera crosses after him in January.
stops.quote: So you plan to go to America again next winter.... When will you ever have time to rest and to compose?
stops.quote_source: Catherine Stravinsky, letter to Igor Stravinsky, 11 March 1935
suggested_refs: The Stravinsky family correspondence of the 1930s, published in Robert Craft's edition of the Selected Correspondence
sources: 'Catherine and Igor Stravinsky,' The New York Review of Books, 22 November 1979

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts: the Norton lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Charles Eliot Norton lectures ran October 1939 to April 1940 and were published as Poetique musicale (1941) and Poetics of Music in the Form of Six Lessons (1947). The authorship of the polished text is established as substantially Roland-Manuel's and Souvtchinsky's.
stops.campa: As Charles Eliot Norton Professor he delivers six lectures in French on the poetics of music: on order set against chaos, on the constraint the composer chooses in order to be free inside it, on the distance between a musician and a man improvising. The prose is elegant and mostly not his own. Alexis Roland-Manuel and Pierre Souvtchinsky drafted the text out of his notes and his conversation, a fact the published book does not disclose and the correspondence later makes plain. The doctrine is his.
suggested_refs: Poetique musicale (1941) and Poetics of Music in the Form of Six Lessons (1947)

segments.name: Hollywood, the Anthem, and the Rows

stops.name: Bedford, Massachusetts: the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested: 9 March 1940 at Bedford, Massachusetts, one year and one week after Catherine's death.
stops.campa: One year and one week after Catherine's death he marries Vera de Bosset, on the ninth of March, in a small town outside Boston, nineteen years after she became his mistress. Catherine had known about Vera from nearly the beginning and had written to her; the letters between the two women survive in the Sacher collection. This second marriage lasts thirty-one years, until his death. The couple travel west to California afterwards, and he applies for naturalisation.
suggested_refs: The Catherine Stravinsky and Vera de Bosset correspondence, in the Paul Sacher Foundation collection
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: West Hollywood: 1260 North Wetherly Drive
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence 1941-1969; month and day are not established and are defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A small house on a hillside above Sunset Boulevard, with a garden and a study, in a Los Angeles that holds the same emigration he belongs to: Thomas Mann, Aldous Huxley, and Arnold Schoenberg ten minutes off in Brentwood. He and Schoenberg live in the same suburb for eleven years and hardly speak. Hollywood asks him for film scores and the negotiations always collapse over control. He writes the Symphony in Three Movements at this table and calls it his war symphony.
suggested_refs: The Stravinsky house at 1260 North Wetherly Drive, West Hollywood, 1941-1969
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Boston: the anthem reharmonised
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the police warning of January 1944 is treated as real in the scholarship, but the pool could not load a primary account and the exact venue is unconfirmed. The photograph circulated as a mug shot is an unrelated 1940 alien-registration portrait; that identification is also carried at R.
stops.campa: He conducts his own reharmonisation of The Star-Spangled Banner with the Boston Symphony, having reset the anthem in a way he considered an improvement on its harmony. The police inform him that Massachusetts law forbids tampering with the national anthem. He drops it from the remaining concerts. There is no arrest and no prosecution. The photograph circulated ever since as his mug shot is an alien-registration portrait taken in 1940 for the immigration authorities.
suggested_refs: Stravinsky's 1941 arrangement of The Star-Spangled Banner, and his 1940 alien-registration photograph
sources: dossier, igor_stravinsky, myth-assessment section (reconstruction: contemporaneous press accounts not independently verified)

stops.name: New York: Orpheus and the young conductor
stops.date_confidence: attested that Orpheus was made with Balanchine and Isamu Noguchi for Ballet Society and premiered in 1948, and that Stravinsky met Robert Craft around the same period; the exact premiere day is not established in the pool.
stops.campa: George Balanchine's Ballet Society gives Orpheus, with Isamu Noguchi's masks and rocks and a score in which the lyre is a harp and the descent to the underworld is a slow procession over a held chord. Composer and choreographer work it out bar by bar in one room, one counting and one timing. In the same season a conductor of twenty-four named Robert Craft writes asking to borrow orchestral parts, and is taken into the house. He stays twenty-three years and ends as executor of the estate.
suggested_refs: Orpheus, Ballet Society, 1948, with Isamu Noguchi's designs

stops.name: Venice, Teatro La Fenice: The Rake's Progress
stops.date_confidence: attested: 11 September 1951 at La Fenice, with Robert Rounseville, Elisabeth Schwarzkopf and Otakar Kraus.
stops.campa: The Rake's Progress opens at La Fenice on a libretto by W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman out of Hogarth's engravings: harpsichord recitative, closed numbers, a graveyard card game played for a soul, and a moral sung straight out at the audience before the curtain. Elisabeth Schwarzkopf sings Anne Trulove. The composer conducts. Robert Craft is at his elbow through the rehearsals. It is the largest thing he ever wrote and the end of the manner he had worked in for thirty years. He is sixty-nine.
suggested_refs: The Rake's Progress, Teatro La Fenice, 11 September 1951

stops.name: West Hollywood: the rows arrive late
stops.date_confidence: attested that In Memoriam Dylan Thomas, completed 1954, is his first work built wholly on twelve-tone technique, and that it followed the death of Dylan Thomas in November 1953 and the collapse of a planned opera with him. Month and day of composition are not established.
stops.campa: Craft puts Webern's scores on the piano in the Wetherly Drive house and conducts Schoenberg where Stravinsky can hear it, three years after Schoenberg's death and a few miles from where he lived. At seventy-two Stravinsky begins writing with rows. He had planned an opera with Dylan Thomas about the rebuilding of the world after a catastrophe, and Thomas died in New York in November 1953 before a line of it was written. In Memoriam Dylan Thomas is the first piece built entirely on a series: five notes, a tenor, a string quartet and four trombones.
suggested_refs: In Memoriam Dylan Thomas (1954), Stravinsky's first fully serial work

stops.name: Washington: dinner at the White House
stops.date_confidence: attested: 18 January 1962, a dinner given by President Kennedy in Stravinsky's honour in the year of his eightieth birthday. The Elegy for J.F.K. was composed in 1964, not 1963: the assassination is of November 1963 and the piece belongs to the following year.
stops.campa: John F. Kennedy gives a dinner in his honour in the year he turns eighty. He has been an American citizen for seventeen years and has outlived nearly every man who commissioned him. Two years afterwards, following Dallas, he sets four lines by W. H. Auden as an elegy for the president: a baritone, three clarinets, under two minutes end to end, and no passage in it that raises its voice. Through these same years he conducts and records his own catalogue.
stops.quote: My music is best understood by children and animals.
stops.quote_source: Stravinsky, interview in The Observer, 8 October 1961
suggested_refs: Elegy for J.F.K. (1964), text by W. H. Auden, for baritone and three clarinets

stops.name: Moscow: received by the state that banned him
stops.date_confidence: attested to September and October 1962, six performances across Moscow and Leningrad, with a reception by Nikita Khrushchev. The exact concert dates and halls are not established in the pool; the Moscow Conservatory Great Hall coordinate is used as the best estimate.
stops.campa: Half a century after he left, the Soviet Union asks him back, and the eighty-year-old conducts in Moscow to a hall that has been officially forbidden his music for most of his life. Khrushchev receives him. Shostakovich and Khachaturian come to listen. He is greeted as a Russian composer by a state that spent decades calling him a formalist and a lackey of the West, and he accepts the greeting without retracting a note or a word of anything. Six performances are given between the two cities.
suggested_refs: The 1962 Soviet tour, Stravinsky's first return to Russia since 1914
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: Leningrad: the city under the other name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the same September-October 1962 journey; the exact Leningrad concert dates and hall are not established in the pool and the Philharmonia Grand Hall coordinate is used as the best estimate. The day given here orders the segment and is not documented.
stops.campa: The city he was born beside is called Leningrad now. He conducts in the Grand Hall, walks streets he last saw in 1914, and is taken to look at the house on the Kryukov Canal where he grew up. He says afterwards that the smell of a Russian city was the thing he had not expected to recognise. Neither Oranienbaum nor Ustyluh is on the itinerary; one is a suburb of a closed naval zone and the other is in another country. The audience will not let him off the platform.
suggested_refs: The Stravinsky family apartment on the Kryukov Canal, Saint Petersburg

stops.name: Toronto, Massey Hall: the last podium
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the venue: a final public conducting appearance in Toronto in 1967, leading Pulcinella, is well attested in the secondary literature, but the pool could not confirm the hall or the day, both of which are best estimates here.
stops.campa: He conducts in public for the last time, leading the suite from Pulcinella, the score with which the neoclassical decades began forty-seven years earlier. Arterial strokes and a failing circulation have taken the rest of the programme, which Craft conducts, as Craft has increasingly done for years. Requiem Canticles, finished the previous autumn, is the last score of any size he completes: nine short movements, a postlude of bells and chords, no soloist given a name. In 1970 the household takes rooms at Evian, on the French shore of Lake Geneva.
suggested_refs: Requiem Canticles (1966), performed at the composer's own funeral
sources: Boosey and Hawkes composer timeline, Igor Stravinsky

stops.name: New York, 920 Fifth Avenue: the last week
stops.date_confidence: attested: hospitalised with pulmonary edema 18-28 March 1971, discharged into a newly prepared Fifth Avenue apartment, the edema recurring on 4 April; died 6 April 1971 at 5.20 a.m. The hospital identification as Lenox Hill is carried at R in the pool.
stops.campa: Ten days in hospital with pulmonary edema, the eighteenth of March to the twenty-eighth, then discharge into an apartment on Fifth Avenue he has occupied for one week. The Californian house was given up in 1969. On the fourth of April the edema returns and Vera decides against sending him back; he stops taking food and drink. At twenty past five on the morning of the sixth he dies, eighty-eight years old. He had asked to be buried in Venice. The body is flown to Italy nine days later.
suggested_refs: The apartment at 920 Fifth Avenue, New York, occupied one week

stops.name: Venice, Santi Giovanni e Paolo: the Orthodox rite
stops.date_confidence: the funeral service at the Basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo on 15 April 1971 is carried by the pool from the Stravinsky article and the dossier; no page reached in this pass independently confirmed the church or the date, and it is left standing with that gap named.
stops.campa: The Orthodox rite is sung for him in the great Dominican basilica of Venice: a Catholic church holding a Russian funeral for a man who died an American citizen in New York. The Requiem Canticles he finished five years earlier are performed over the coffin. He had conducted in this city, and the Rake's Progress opened here twenty years before. Venice has no claim on him except the one he made himself. Gondolas wait on the canal outside to carry him north across the lagoon.
suggested_refs: The Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo, Venice, site of the funeral service
sources: dossier, igor_stravinsky, basic-facts summary (church and date not independently confirmed)

stops.name: Isola di San Michele: the Orthodox ground
stops.date_confidence: attested: buried 15 April 1971 in the Orthodox section of the San Michele cemetery island, near Diaghilev's grave, which is confirmed from the Diaghilev side. Vera de Bosset was buried there in 1982. The coordinate is the canonical San Michele pin already used in the atlas.
stops.campa: The coffin crosses the lagoon and is carried into the Orthodox enclosure, where the Russians who died out of Russia are buried. Sergei Diaghilev, who wanted an unknown for his second Paris season and got The Firebird, has lain a few paces off since 1929. Vera de Bosset joins Stravinsky in 1982. In Paris in 1983, beside the Pompidou, a shallow basin of sixteen coloured mechanical sculptures is dedicated and named for him: a firebird, a nightingale, Petrushka, all of them spitting water.
suggested_refs: The Orthodox enclosure of the Cimitero di San Michele, Venice
